questions.q: Which of these belongs in Git for a dbt project?
options: The models/, tests/, and macros/ folders — hand-written source code
The target/ folder — dbt's compiled output
The dbt_packages/ folder — downloaded package dependencies
The logs/ folder
questions.explain: models/, tests/, and macros/ contain hand-written source; target/, dbt_packages/, and logs/ are all regenerated automatically and should be ignored.

questions.q: Why shouldn't dbt's target/ directory be committed to Git?
options: It's regenerated automatically every run, so committing it creates merge conflicts on files nobody hand-edits
Git physically cannot store compiled SQL files
It contains no useful information whatsoever
dbt requires it to be deleted before every commit
questions.explain: Since target/ regenerates on every dbt run, committing it adds noise and merge conflicts without adding real history.

questions.q: What does this lesson recommend for organizing notebooks in a repository that also has a dbt project?
options: Keep them in a dedicated top-level notebooks/ folder, separate from models/
Scatter them throughout the models/ folder for convenience
Convert every notebook into a dbt model immediately
Never allow notebooks in the same repository as a dbt project
questions.explain: A dedicated notebooks/ folder keeps exploration visually separate from production dbt models in the file tree.

questions.q: How should raw .sql files outside of a dbt project be versioned, according to this lesson?
options: Exactly like any other text file, organized into folders by purpose (analysis/, migrations/, reports/)
They cannot be tracked by Git at all
Only inside a dbt project, never on their own
As binary files requiring Git LFS
questions.explain: SQL is plain text and diffs perfectly well on its own — the only real decision is organizing files by purpose rather than one flat folder.

questions.q: What four things does this lesson's sanity checklist ask you to confirm before committing to a data repository?
options: Generated dirs ignored, credentials ignored, large datasets handled via LFS or an object store, and notebooks have cleared outputs or nbdime configured
That every file is under 10 lines long
That the repository has no branches other than main
That every commit message is exactly one word
questions.explain: The checklist ties together every lesson in this chapter: .gitignore for generated output and secrets, LFS or an object store for large files, and clean notebook diffs.
